reading.rtitle: Why a Protocol Is Written Like That
paras: A protocol reads like nothing else you will meet in English. There are no opinions in it, almost no full subjects, and the sentences are so short that a first reader assumes something is missing. Nothing is missing. A protocol is written by somebody who has already made every mistake it is trying to stop you making, and every word in it is doing a job. Learn to read six kinds of sentence and the whole document opens: the instruction, the order, the condition, the warning, the quantity and the exception.

The instruction is the backbone, and it never names you. Add the reagent. Dilute the sample. Incubate for twenty minutes. There is no I, no you and no we, because the protocol is not describing what somebody did, it is telling the next person what to do. This is the single most common reason a first-year student reads a protocol twice: the sentence starts with a verb, and the eye is looking for a subject that will never come.

Order and condition carry the rest. First, weigh out the powder. Then make up the solution. Once the mixture is clear, incubate the tubes. Before you start, label every tube. Do not rinse the glassware until the batch is complete. Those small words are not decoration and they are not interchangeable: after and once tell you that something has to have happened already, while before and until tell you where a step stops. A protocol that says allow the tubes to stand for five minutes before adding the reagent is describing a different experiment from one that says add the reagent, then allow the tubes to stand.

Then there are the two sentences that are not about chemistry at all. The warning tells you where the hazard is, and it is almost always written as must or must not, which is stronger than should and is not a suggestion: waste must be discarded in the marked container, this reagent must not be handled outside the fume hood. And the exception is the one that catches everybody, because it is usually a single word buried in the middle of a step. Rinse thoroughly, except after the final incubation. If you read a protocol at speed and miss one word, that is usually the word.

choices: Protocols are badly written and should be rewritten in normal English
A protocol is six recognisable kinds of sentence, and reading it is learning to tell them apart

items: A protocol sentence usually starts with a verb and has no subject.
There is no I, no you and no we, because the protocol is telling the next person what to do, not describing what somebody did.
Before and until mean the same thing as after and once.
After and once tell you that something has to have happened already, while before and until tell you where a step stops.
Must not is only a strong suggestion in a protocol.
It is stronger than should and is not a suggestion. It marks where the hazard is.
The order of two steps can change the experiment.
Allow the tubes to stand for five minutes before adding the reagent describes a different experiment from add the reagent, then allow the tubes to stand.
Exceptions are always written in a separate paragraph at the end.
The exception is usually a single word buried in the middle of a step, which is why it catches everybody.

listenings.text: Right, everybody, this is the induction and it takes four minutes, so please do not start unpacking yet. Three rules, and they are the three that people break in their first fortnight. Rule one. Label every tube before you fill it, not after. I know that sounds obvious and I have thrown away an entire afternoon of somebody else's work because four identical tubes came back to the rack with nothing written on them. Rule two. Waste goes in the marked container by the door and nowhere else. Not the sink, not the general bin, not a beaker you are planning to deal with later. Rule three, and this is the one that matters most. If a protocol says a reagent must not be handled outside the fume hood, that is not a recommendation and it is not there because somebody is being careful. Somebody was hurt, and the sentence was added afterwards. If you are not sure whether a step applies to you, stop and ask. Nobody in this building has ever been annoyed by that question.

Hi, it is me, listen, do not run the protocol the way it is printed, I meant to catch you before you left yesterday. Step four changed last month and the copy on the bench is the old one. So: weigh out the powder as normal, that part is the same, but make up the solution with the buffer from the fridge and not the one on the shelf. They look identical and the labels are almost the same, which is exactly the problem. Then, and this is the actual change, allow the tubes to stand for five minutes before you add the reagent. The old version had you adding it straight away and the batch came out cloudy every single time. After that, incubate for twenty minutes as usual. One more thing, and then I will let you go. Do not rinse the glassware until the whole batch is finished, because if you rinse halfway through you will have nothing to compare the last four tubes against. Text me when you are done.
